content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is the most common bacterial infection in young children in the United States. There are significant limitations and concerns regarding the use of antibiotics and surgical interventions for its treatment, which makes effective preventative strategies highly desirable. Xylitol, a natural sugar substitute known for its ability to reduce dental decay, has been proposed as a potential preventative measure. In vitro studies have demonstrated that xylitol can inhibit the adherence of Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae to nasopharyngeal cells. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of xylitol in preventing AOM in children aged 12 years or younger. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases, such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts, covering publications up to January 2016. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs comparing xylitol supplementation with placebo or no treatment for the prevention of AOM in this population. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their quality, and extracted relevant data. They also contacted study authors to obtain missing information. Data on adverse events associated with xylitol were recorded, and the effect size was calculated using risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Five clinical trials involving a total of 3405 children were included in the review. For the 2016 update, one new trial was identified and systematically reviewed, but it was excluded from the meta-analysis due to significant heterogeneity. The remaining four trials were deemed to have adequate methodological quality. Three RCTs, involving 1826 healthy Finnish children attending daycare, provided moderate-quality evidence that xylitol, in any form, reduced the risk of AOM from 30% to approximately 22% compared to the control group (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88). There were no significant differences in adverse events, such as abdominal discomfort or rash, between the xylitol and control groups. However, xylitol was not effective in reducing AOM in healthy children during respiratory infections (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.53; moderate-quality evidence) or in otitis-prone healthy children (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.21; low-quality evidence). In conclusion, there is moderate-quality evidence suggesting that prophylactic administration of xylitol can reduce the incidence of AOM in healthy children attending daycare centers. However, the evidence is inconclusive regarding its efficacy in preventing AOM in children with respiratory infections or in otitis-prone children. The meta-analysis was limited by the small number of studies available, most of which were conducted by the same research group.
